vignette:
The Weight Behind the Screen

Kofi is a 33-year-old Ghanaian man who spent fourteen months working as a logistics coordinator for a humanitarian relief organization in South Sudan, returning home to his wife, Abena, nearly two years ago. He now works as a social media manager for a mid-sized marketing firm in Accra, spending his days crafting content calendars and monitoring engagement metrics - a life that looks, from the outside, almost deliberately ordinary.

In South Sudan, Kofi was responsible for coordinating food and medical supply routes through contested territories. He witnessed things that do not belong in any vocabulary he was raised with: a convoy ambush that killed two colleagues he had briefed that same morning, the distribution center attack that left him sheltering beneath a metal table for three hours while gunfire moved closer and then, inexplicably, farther away. He remembers the smell of the room - diesel and rust - more vividly than he remembers his wedding day. He came home with a duffel bag and what his wife initially described as "quietness," a word that has since grown heavier with each passing month.

At work, Kofi is competent and well-liked. He is good at his job. But managing social media means he is exposed to an unfiltered stream of the world's imagery, and the algorithm does not know what he has seen. A news clip shared on a client's feed - a burning building, a crowd running - can send him somewhere he cannot name in under a second. His heart rate spikes before his mind has registered why. He has learned to keep a glass of water on his desk at all times, something to hold, something cold and real. His colleagues assume he is simply focused.

At home, the picture is different. Kofi sleeps on his side of the bed with a rigidity that Abena has stopped commenting on. He wakes between two and four in the morning, sometimes sitting upright, sometimes already standing near the window without knowing how he got there. The dreams are not always dramatic - sometimes it is simply the table, the floor, the sound - but he wakes from them drenched and certain, for several disorienting seconds, that he is still there. He does not tell Abena what the dreams contain. He tells her he is fine, that he just needs water, and she watches him from the doorway with an expression he cannot bear to look at directly.

He has stopped attending the church they used to go to together. The congregation is large and sometimes the worship music swells unexpectedly, and once, six months ago, he walked out during a service and sat in the car for forty minutes, hands on the steering wheel, engine off. He told Abena the room was too warm. She did not argue.

Kofi finds himself scanning rooms when he enters them - exits, windows, the positioning of other people. He does this at the supermarket, at restaurants, at his in-laws' home during Sunday dinners. He is aware that it is not rational. He does it anyway. He has declined three work trips, including one to Lagos that would have been a significant career opportunity, because the thought of an unfamiliar city, an unfamiliar hotel, produces a dread he cannot rationalize away.

He describes himself, when asked, as someone who is "readjusting." He uses the word carefully, as though it is a container he has chosen for its neutral shape. He believes he should be over this by now. He went to help people - he did not fight, he did not carry a weapon, and he returned home intact. He struggles to extend to himself the same compassion he would offer without hesitation to anyone else who had lived through what he lived through.

Most evenings, after Abena has gone to bed, Kofi sits in the kitchen with his laptop, scheduling posts for tomorrow, the blue light of the screen the only light in the house.
